claim: Animals make small unexplained movements on top of primary task-related motions while tracking or searching for targets.
source: While animals track or search for targets, sensory organs make small unexplained movements on top of the primary task-related motions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general observation about animal behavior.

claim: Multiple theories exist for sensing movements including infotaxis, gain adaptation, spectral whitening, and high-pass filtering.
source: While multiple theories for these movements exist—in that they support infotaxis, gain adaptation, spectral whitening, and high-pass filtering—predicted trajectories show poor fit to measured trajectories.
evidence: The abstract cites existing theories in the literature.

claim: Predicted trajectories from existing theories show poor fit to measured trajectories.
source: While multiple theories for these movements exist—in that they support infotaxis, gain adaptation, spectral whitening, and high-pass filtering—predicted trajectories show poor fit to measured trajectories.
evidence: This is a comparative claim made in the abstract based on the study's findings.

claim: Energy-constrained proportional betting is a new theory where the probability of moving to a location is proportional to an expectation of how informative it will be balanced against the movement's predicted energetic cost.
source: We propose a new theory for these movements called energy-constrained proportional betting, where the probability of moving to a location is proportional to an expectation of how informative it will be balanced against the movement's predicted energetic cost.
evidence: This is the main theoretical contribution stated in the abstract.

claim: Trajectories generated by energy-constrained proportional betting show good agreement with measured trajectories of fish tracking an object using electrosense.
source: Trajectories generated in this way show good agreement with measured trajectories of fish tracking an object using electrosense, a mammal and an insect localizing an odor source, and a moth tracking a flower using vision.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data throughout the paper.

claim: Trajectories generated by energy-constrained proportional betting show good agreement with measured trajectories of a mammal localizing an odor source.
source: Trajectories generated in this way show good agreement with measured trajectories of fish tracking an object using electrosense, a mammal and an insect localizing an odor source, and a moth tracking a flower using vision.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data throughout the paper.

claim: Trajectories generated by energy-constrained proportional betting show good agreement with measured trajectories of an insect localizing an odor source.
source: Trajectories generated in this way show good agreement with measured trajectories of fish tracking an object using electrosense, a mammal and an insect localizing an odor source, and a moth tracking a flower using vision.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data throughout the paper.

claim: Trajectories generated by energy-constrained proportional betting show good agreement with measured trajectories of a moth tracking a flower using vision.
source: Trajectories generated in this way show good agreement with measured trajectories of fish tracking an object using electrosense, a mammal and an insect localizing an odor source, and a moth tracking a flower using vision.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data throughout the paper.

claim: The theory unifies the metabolic cost of motion with information theory.
source: Our theory unifies the metabolic cost of motion with information theory.
evidence: This is a claim about the theoretical contribution made in the abstract.

claim: The theory predicts sense organ movements in animals.
source: It predicts sense organ movements in animals and can prescribe sensor motion for robots to enhance performance.
evidence: This is stated as a capability of the theory in the abstract.

claim: The theory can prescribe sensor motion for robots to enhance performance.
source: It predicts sense organ movements in animals and can prescribe sensor motion for robots to enhance performance.
evidence: This is stated as a capability of the theory in the abstract.

claim: Movement can be used to obtain information that is unevenly distributed in the environment.
source: Movement can be used to obtain information that is unevenly distributed in the environment.
evidence: This is a general principle stated in the introduction.

claim: Movement is energetically costly.
source: Because movement is energetically costly, there is likely a balance between the benefits of increased sensory information and energetic costs for obtaining that information (MacIver et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: There is likely a balance between the benefits of increased sensory information and energetic costs for obtaining that information.
source: Because movement is energetically costly, there is likely a balance between the benefits of increased sensory information and energetic costs for obtaining that information (MacIver et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis supported by a citation.

claim: Sensory organs or animals undergo small and seemingly extraneous movements as they near or track a target of interest.
source: This theory, energy-constrained proportional betting, predicts the small and seemingly extraneous movements that sensory organs or animals undergo as they near or track a target of interest (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Martin, 1965; Basil et al., 2000; Ferner and Weissburg, 2005; Webb et al., 2004; Willis and Avondet, 2005; Porter et al., 2007; Louis et al., 2008; Duistermars et al., 2009; Yovel et al., 2010; Khan et al., 2012; Stamper et al., 2012; Catania, 2013; Sponberg et al., 2015; Lockey and Willis, 2015; Rucci and Victor, 2015; Stöckl et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as an observed phenomenon with multiple citations and reference to a figure.

claim: These movements appear unrelated to the movements that are necessary to achieve the task at hand.
source: These movements appear unrelated to the movements that are necessary to achieve the task at hand.
evidence: This is an observational claim made in the introduction.

claim: Weakly electric fish will track and stay near a moving refuge.
source: For example, weakly electric fish will track and stay near a moving refuge, but in addition to the large motions needed to stay near the refuge, there are small whole-body oscillations—an electrosensory analog to microsaccades (Video 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Stamper et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as an example with citation and reference to video and figure.

claim: In addition to large motions needed to stay near the refuge, weakly electric fish have small whole-body oscillations.
source: For example, weakly electric fish will track and stay near a moving refuge, but in addition to the large motions needed to stay near the refuge, there are small whole-body oscillations—an electrosensory analog to microsaccades (Video 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Stamper et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as an example with citation and reference to video and figure.

claim: Small whole-body oscillations in weakly electric fish are an electrosensory analog to microsaccades.
source: For example, weakly electric fish will track and stay near a moving refuge, but in addition to the large motions needed to stay near the refuge, there are small whole-body oscillations—an electrosensory analog to microsaccades (Video 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Stamper et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as an analogy with citation and reference to video and figure.

claim: Animals vary their sampling frequency or the location at which samples are taken in behaviors where animals sample discretely over time.
source: Similarly, in behaviors where animals sample discretely over time, animals vary their sampling frequency or the location at which samples are taken, as observed in bats, rats, beaked whales, humans, and pulse electric fish (Yovel et al., 2010; Mitchinson et al., 2007; Hartmann, 2001; Kothari et al., 2018; Caputi et al., 2003; Pluta and Kawasaki, 2008; Nelson and MacIver, 2006; Schnitzler et al., 2003; Madsen et al., 2005; Yang et al., 2016; Hoppe and Rothkopf, 2019).
evidence: This is stated as an observed phenomenon with multiple citations.

claim: Several theories have been proposed to account for sensing movements including information maximization or infotaxis.
source: There have been several theories proposed to account for these sensing movements including information maximization or infotaxis (Figure 1; Najemnik and Geisler, 2005; Vergassola et al., 2007; Yovel et al., 2010; Calhoun et al., 2014; Álvarez-Salvado et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2016), gain adaptation (Stöckl et al., 2017; Biswas et al., 2018), spectral whitening (Rucci and Victor, 2015), and high-pass filtering (Stamper et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations and reference to a figure.

claim: Several theories have been proposed to account for sensing movements including gain adaptation.
source: There have been several theories proposed to account for these sensing movements including information maximization or infotaxis (Figure 1; Najemnik and Geisler, 2005; Vergassola et al., 2007; Yovel et al., 2010; Calhoun et al., 2014; Álvarez-Salvado et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2016), gain adaptation (Stöckl et al., 2017; Biswas et al., 2018), spectral whitening (Rucci and Victor, 2015), and high-pass filtering (Stamper et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations and reference to a figure.

claim: Several theories have been proposed to account for sensing movements including spectral whitening.
source: There have been several theories proposed to account for these sensing movements including information maximization or infotaxis (Figure 1; Najemnik and Geisler, 2005; Vergassola et al., 2007; Yovel et al., 2010; Calhoun et al., 2014; Álvarez-Salvado et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2016), gain adaptation (Stöckl et al., 2017; Biswas et al., 2018), spectral whitening (Rucci and Victor, 2015), and high-pass filtering (Stamper et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations and reference to a figure.

claim: Several theories have been proposed to account for sensing movements including high-pass filtering.
source: There have been several theories proposed to account for these sensing movements including information maximization or infotaxis (Figure 1; Najemnik and Geisler, 2005; Vergassola et al., 2007; Yovel et al., 2010; Calhoun et al., 2014; Álvarez-Salvado et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2016), gain adaptation (Stöckl et al., 2017; Biswas et al., 2018), spectral whitening (Rucci and Victor, 2015), and high-pass filtering (Stamper et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations and reference to a figure.

claim: Most existing theories are underspecified in that they do not attempt to provide a complete control framework and are therefore incapable of generating realistic trajectories for direct behavioral validation.
source: However, most existing theories are underspecified in that they do not attempt to provide a complete control framework and are therefore incapable of generating realistic trajectories for direct behavioral validation (Discussion).
evidence: This is a critical assessment of existing theories made in the introduction.

claim: An implementation of energy-constrained proportional betting generates trajectories with good agreement to measured behavior.
source: We show that an implementation of energy-constrained proportional betting generates trajectories with good agreement to measured behavior.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction.

claim: The peak expected information is typically not at the same location as the object.
source: Because the peak expected information is typically not at the same location as the object, we illustrate the target peak as the point of maximum target visibility.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 1A.

claim: Information maximization locally maximizes the expected information density at every step.
source: Trajectories generated by information maximization (entropy minimization) locally maximizes the expected information density (EID) at every step, which here commands a path straight to the nearby distractor.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 1B describing the behavior of information maximization.

claim: Information maximization commands a path straight to the nearby distractor in the scenario shown.
source: Trajectories generated by information maximization (entropy minimization) locally maximizes the expected information density (EID) at every step, which here commands a path straight to the nearby distractor.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 1B and shown in the figure.

claim: Energy-constrained proportional betting samples the EID proportionate to its density and is balanced by the cost of movement.
source: In contrast, energy-constrained proportional betting (C) samples the EID proportionate to its density and is balanced by the cost of movement.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 1C describing the behavior of energy-constrained proportional betting.

claim: The natural trade-off between exploration and exploitation that emerges from energy-constrained proportional betting leads to localization of the target and rejection of the distractor.
source: The natural trade-off between exploration and exploitation that emerges leads to localization of the target and rejection of the distractor (adapted from Figure 3 of Miller et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 1C with citation.

claim: The expected information is higher along the high slope region of the belief because in this region, small changes in location is expected to cause large changes in the received sensory signal and hence carry more information about position.
source: Intuitively, the expected information is higher along the high slope region of the belief because in this region, small changes in location (x axis direction in the upper inset) is expected to cause large changes in the received sensory signal and hence carry more information about position.
evidence: This is an explanation provided in the caption of Figure 1D.

claim: Energy-constrained proportional betting results in persistent activation of movement when the EID is relatively diffuse due to lack of information.
source: Energy-constrained proportional betting results in persistent activation of movement when the EID is relatively diffuse due to lack of information.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 1E describing simulation results.

claim: Ergodic information harvesting responded to the distractor by making a detour away from the actual target position to gamble on the chance of acquiring more information but does not get trapped by the distractor because of the proportional betting strategy in combination with the transient nature of fictive distractors.
source: As seen by the digression at the arrow, ergodic information harvesting (EIH) responded to the distractor by making a detour away from the actual target position to gamble on the chance of acquiring more information but does not get trapped by the distractor because of the proportional betting strategy in combination with the transient nature of fictive distractors.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 1E describing simulation results.

claim: Under strong signal conditions, the energy-constrained proportional betting trajectory samples both peaks of the bimodal EID with excursions away from these peaks, similar to measured moth behavior.
source: Same as (E), but under strong signal conditions. Now the energy-constrained proportional betting trajectory samples both peaks of the bimodal EID with excursions away from these peaks, similar to measured moth behavior (Stöckl et al., 2017, see Figure 1—figure supplement 1 'Moth').
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 1F with citation and reference to another figure.

claim: Sensing-related movements occur with striking consistency across animals using different sensory modalities and within different physical environments.
source: These sensing-related movements occur with striking consistency across animals using different sensory modalities and within different physical environments.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The expected information density represents how much information about the state of a target will be gained by moving sensory organs to a given location.
source: Across several methods for computing predictive trajectories of animals tracking targets, an important quantity is the expected information density representing how much information about the state of a target will be gained by moving sensory organs to a given location (EID; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a definition provided in the introduction with reference to a figure.

claim: Infotaxis generates trajectories that maximize expected information by commanding motion toward a peak of the EID.
source: A method called infotaxis (Vergassola et al., 2007) similarly generates trajectories that maximize expected information by commanding motion toward a peak of the EID.
evidence: This is stated as a description of infotaxis with citation.

claim: Expected information maximization leads to problems when there is a high level of uncertainty, as is frequently the case in naturalistic conditions.
source: However, expected information maximization leads to problems when there is a high level of uncertainty, as is frequently the case in naturalistic conditions.
evidence: This is a critical assessment made in the introduction.

claim: If the gain of information in all directions is low, the prescribed action of information maximization is to stay in place.
source: One problem is that if the gain of information in all directions is low, the prescribed action is to stay in place; yet, animals rarely opt for immobility in the absence of signal.
evidence: This is stated as a problem with information maximization.

claim: Animals rarely opt for immobility in the absence of signal.
source: One problem is that if the gain of information in all directions is low, the prescribed action is to stay in place; yet, animals rarely opt for immobility in the absence of signal.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about animal behavior.

claim: Information maximization is susceptible to distractors.
source: Another problem is susceptibility to distractors.
evidence: This is stated as a problem with information maximization.

claim: A distractor can be either a real physical object which appears similar to the desired target, or a transient target-like appearance caused by noise.
source: A distractor can be either a real physical object which appears similar to the desired target, or a transient target-like appearance caused by noise.
evidence: This is a definition provided in the introduction.

claim: Because the gradient of increased expected information leads to the distractor, the sensor is commanded to go straight to it with information maximization, potentially ignoring other signal information related to the intended target.
source: Because the gradient of increased expected information leads to the distractor, the sensor is commanded to go straight to it, potentially ignoring other signal information related to the intended target.
evidence: This is stated as a description of information maximization behavior with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: With energy-constrained proportional betting, sensory organs are moved to sample spatially distributed signals proportionate to the EID, balanced by the energetic cost of the movement.
source: In contrast to the expected information maximizing solution, with energy-constrained proportional betting, sensory organs (or signal emitters in the case of animals like bats and electric fish) are moved to sample spatially distributed signals proportionate to the EID, as shown in Figure 1C, balanced by the energetic cost of the movement.
evidence: This is a description of energy-constrained proportional betting with reference to a figure.

claim: The underlying sensory sampling strategy gambles on the chance of obtaining more information at a given location through carefully controlled sensor motion that balances proportionally betting on the expected information gain and minimizing the energy expended for motion.
source: The underlying sensory sampling strategy gambles on the chance of obtaining more information at a given location through carefully controlled sensor motion that balances two factors that typically push in opposite directions: (1) proportionally bet on the expected information gain (that is, take more samples by moving slowly in high EID regions and fewer samples by moving more rapidly in low EID regions); and (2) minimize the energy expended for motion.
evidence: This is a description of the sensory sampling strategy.

claim: A key behavioral signature of energy-constrained proportional betting is an increase in the magnitude of sensing-related movements as signal weakens or signal noise increases.
source: This illustrates a key behavioral signature of energy-constrained proportional betting—an increase in the magnitude of sensing-related movements as signal weakens or signal noise increases.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction of the theory.

claim: With no sensory input, there is uniform probability that the target is anywhere in the space, resulting in an energy-constrained trajectory that spans the entire space.
source: With no sensory input, there is uniform probability that the target is anywhere in the space, resulting in an energy-constrained trajectory that spans the entire space.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction of the theory.

claim: Information maximization such as infotaxis leads to cessation of motion under very weak signals.
source: This contrasts with the cessation of motion that occurs under very weak signals with an information maximization strategy such as infotaxis (see Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a contrast with reference to a figure.

claim: The expected information of sensing locations is quantified by how much an observation at a location would reduce the Shannon-Weaver entropy of the current estimate of the target's location.
source: For this study we have quantified the expected information of sensing locations by how much an observation at a location would reduce the Shannon-Weaver entropy (hereafter entropy) of the current estimate of the target's location, as in infotaxis (Vergassola et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological choice with citation.

claim: Other measures of information such as Fisher Information can be used with near identical results.
source: However, other measures of information such as Fisher Information can be used with near identical results (Miller et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as an alternative approach with citation.

claim: The ergodic metric provides a way of comparing a trajectory to a distribution by asking whether a trajectory over some time interval has the same spatial statistics as a given distribution.
source: The ergodic metric provides a way of comparing a trajectory to a distribution (i.e., in the case of this paper, the EID) by asking whether a trajectory over some time interval has the same spatial statistics as a given distribution (Materials and methods, Appendix 3).
evidence: This is a description of the ergodic metric.

claim: Comparing a trajectory to a distribution is a novel capability of the ergodic metric that is not shared by common methods of comparing two probability distributions.
source: Comparing a trajectory to a distribution is a novel capability of the ergodic metric (Mathew and Mezić, 2011) that is not shared by common methods of comparing two probability distributions (Appendix 2).
evidence: This is stated as a novel capability with citation.

claim: Through optimizing a mathematical function that combines ergodicity with the energy of movement, trajectories are obtained that bet on information balanced by the metabolic cost to move to informative locations in the space.
source: Through optimizing a mathematical function that combines ergodicity with the energy of movement (Algorithm 1), we obtain trajectories that bet on information balanced by the metabolic cost to move to informative locations in the space.
evidence: This is a description of the optimization approach.

claim: With a perfectly ergodic trajectory, the distribution of expected information is perfectly encoded by the trajectory.
source: With a perfectly ergodic trajectory (one with an ergodic measure of zero, only possible with infinite time and when the energy of movement is not constrained), the distribution of expected information is perfectly encoded by the trajectory, or equivalently, the trajectory does perfect proportional betting on the EID.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about perfect ergodicity.

claim: Prior studies have indicated that proportional betting is used at the cognitive decision-making level in primates.
source: While prior studies have indicated that proportional betting is used at the cognitive decision-making level in primates (Monosov et al., 2015; Gottlieb et al., 2014), our results suggest that an energy-constrained form of it occurs more broadly as an embodied component of information processing across a wide phylogenetic bracket.
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: An energy-constrained form of proportional betting occurs more broadly as an embodied component of information processing across a wide phylogenetic bracket.
source: While prior studies have indicated that proportional betting is used at the cognitive decision-making level in primates (Monosov et al., 2015; Gottlieb et al., 2014), our results suggest that an energy-constrained form of it occurs more broadly as an embodied component of information processing across a wide phylogenetic bracket.
evidence: This is a primary claim of the study.

claim: Weakly electric fish engage in a behavior termed refuge tracking where they try to maintain their position inside a close-fitting open-ended enclosure even as that enclosure is translated forward and backward along the lengthwise axis of the fish.
source: Weakly electric fish engage in a behavior termed refuge tracking where they try to maintain their position inside a close-fitting open-ended enclosure—such as a plastic tube—even as that enclosure is translated forward and backward along the lengthwise axis of the fish (Video 1, Rose and Canfield, 1993).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the behavior with citation and reference to video.

claim: Refuge tracking is a natural behavior within protective cover swayed by water flow, such as vegetation or root masses, during the fish's inactive (diurnal) periods in the South American rivers in which they live.
source: Refuge tracking is a natural behavior within protective cover swayed by water flow, such as vegetation or root masses, during the fish's inactive (diurnal) periods in the South American rivers in which they live (Rose and Canfield, 1993).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the natural behavior with citation.

claim: Prior work has shown that as sensory input is degraded, weakly electric fish will engage in larger full-body excursions from the path taken by the refuge.
source: Prior work has shown that as sensory input is degraded, these fish will engage in larger full-body excursions from the path taken by the refuge (Stamper et al., 2012; Biswas et al., 2018; Rose and Canfield, 1993).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: Electrosensory input was degraded through varying the intensity of an externally imposed electrical jamming stimulus.
source: For the trials reported here, all in the dark under infrared illumination, we degraded electrosensory input through varying the intensity of an externally imposed electrical jamming stimulus (Materials and methods) which has previously been shown to impair electrolocation performance (Watanabe and Takeda, 1963; Bastian, 1987; Ramcharitar et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological approach with citations.

claim: The weak signal condition resulted in more body movement during tracking.
source: The weak signal condition (Figure 2D) resulted in more body movement during tracking.
evidence: This is stated as an observation with reference to a figure.

claim: Relative exploration is the amount of movement of the body divided by the minimum amount of movement required for perfect tracking.
source: In order to quantify the increase in movement during tracking, we defined a measure termed relative exploration, which is the amount of movement of the body divided by the minimum amount of movement required for perfect tracking (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a definition of a measure.

claim: Two frequency bands can be identified in the frequency spectrum of the refuge tracking trajectory: a baseline tracking band that overlaps with the frequency at which the target was moved, and a frequency band that accounts for most of the increased exploratory movements as signal weakens.
source: Two frequency bands can be identified: (1) a baseline tracking band that overlaps with the frequency at which the target (the refuge) was moved; and (2) a frequency band that accounts for most of the increased exploratory movements as signal weakens.
evidence: This is stated as an observation with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: The significantly increased relative exploration is primarily from sensing-related movements rather than baseline tracking movements.
source: This confirms that the significantly increased relative exploration reported in Figure 3A is primarily from sensing-related movements rather than baseline tracking movements.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the analysis.

claim: Relative tracking error increases in proportion to the amount of sensing-related motion attenuation.
source: Relative tracking error increases in proportion to the amount of sensing-related motion attenuation, from ≈50% with no attenuation to ≈75% with the highest attenuation we used.
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: An increase in attenuation leads to monotonically increasing distance from ergodicity.
source: We then evaluated the distance from ergodicity, a dimensionless quantity that measures how well a given trajectory matches the corresponding EID distribution (Materials and methods) for all the trajectories. We found that an increase in attenuation also leads to monotonically increasing distance from ergodicity.
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: The filtered trajectories are progressively worse at proportionally betting on information as attenuation increases.
source: This indicates that the filtered trajectories are progressively worse at proportionally betting on information (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the finding with reference to a figure.

claim: The distance from ergodicity is proportional to tracking error.
source: Figure 4C combines these two analyses, demonstrating that the distance from ergodicity is proportional to tracking error.
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to a figure.

claim: The tracking error decreased as the relative energy increased, with diminishing returns as the relative energy level neared that needed for the original unfiltered EIH trajectory.
source: We found that the tracking error decreased as the relative energy increased, with diminishing returns as the relative energy level neared that needed for the original unfiltered EIH trajectory (≈30 times the energy needed to move the body along the sinusoidal refuge trajectory, Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to a figure.

claim: The body's information processing and mechanical systems have coevolved to afford behaviors that enhance evolutionary fitness.
source: The body's information processing and mechanical systems have coevolved to afford behaviors that enhance evolutionary fitness.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle in the discussion.

claim: Shortly after Shannon published his work on the information capacity of communication channels, his ideas were applied to visual perception to describe efficient coding in the visual periphery.
source: Shortly after Shannon published his work on the information capacity of communication channels (Shannon and Weaver, 1949), his ideas were applied to visual perception (Attneave, 1954; Barlow, 1959) to describe efficient coding in the visual periphery.
evidence: This is stated as historical context with citations.

claim: Continual progress has been made in applying information theory to illuminate a host of problems in the coding and energetics of sensory signals from receptors to central nervous system processing.
source: Since then, continual progress has been made in applying information theory to illuminate a host of problems in the coding and energetics of sensory signals from receptors to central nervous system processing (Atick, 1992; Laughlin et al., 1998; Niven and Laughlin, 2008; Sengupta et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as historical context with citations.

claim: A general theory to bridge the gap between the information gained through movement and the energetics of movement is missing.
source: More recently these two areas are coming together in a growing literature that connects the information gathered through movement to the analysis of movement (Körding and Wolpert, 2004; Cowan and Fortune, 2007; Rucci and Victor, 2015; Bush et al., 2016; MacIver et al., 2010; Sprayberry and Daniel, 2007; Stamper et al., 2012; Biswas et al., 2018; Yovel et al., 2010; Stöckl et al., 2017; Fujioka et al., 2016; Yovel et al., 2011; Ghose and Moss, 2003; Hofmann et al., 2014; Bar et al., 2015; Nelson and MacIver, 2006; Bush et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2016), but a general theory to bridge the gap between the information gained through movement and the energetics of movement is missing (MacIver et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature with citations.

claim: Energy-constrained proportional betting is a candidate that is sufficiently general to invite application to a host of information-related movements observed in living organisms.
source: Energy-constrained proportional betting is a candidate that is sufficiently general to invite application to a host of information-related movements observed in living organisms, while its algorithmic instantiation (Algorithm 1) is able to generate testable quantitative predictions.
evidence: This is stated as a claim about the theory.

claim: The algorithmic instantiation of energy-constrained proportional betting is able to generate testable quantitative predictions.
source: Energy-constrained proportional betting is a candidate that is sufficiently general to invite application to a host of information-related movements observed in living organisms, while its algorithmic instantiation (Algorithm 1) is able to generate testable quantitative predictions.
evidence: This is stated as a claim about the algorithm.

claim: In the insects-to-mammals assemblage of animal species analyzed, gambling on information through motion is observed, where the magnitude of the gamble is indexed by the energy it requires.
source: In the insects-to-mammals assemblage of animal species analyzed above, we observe gambling on information through motion, where the magnitude of the gamble is indexed by the energy it requires.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the analysis.

claim: EIH's approach of extremizing a combination of ergodicity and energy generates trajectories that bet on information, exchanging units of energy for the opportunity to obtain a measurement in a new high-value location.
source: EIH's approach of extremizing a combination of ergodicity and energy generates trajectories that bet on information, exchanging units of energy for the opportunity to obtain a measurement in a new high-value location.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the EIH approach.

claim: A key change that occurs as sensory signals weaken is an increase in the rate and amplitude of the excursions from the mean trajectory for both measured and EIH-generated trajectories.
source: For both measured and EIH-generated trajectories, a key change that occurs as sensory signals weaken is an increase in the rate and amplitude of the excursions from the mean trajectory, which we have quantified as an increase in relative exploration.
evidence: This is stated as a finding.

claim: The increase in the size of exploratory excursions in weak signal conditions arises with proportional betting because the EID spreads out in these conditions due to high uncertainty.
source: First, the increase in the size of exploratory excursions in weak signal conditions arises with proportional betting because the EID spreads out in these conditions due to high uncertainty (for example, wider magenta bands in Figure 2I compared to Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated as an explanation with reference to figures.

claim: Because a proportional betting trajectory samples proportionate to the expected information, as the expected information diffuses, the excursions needed for its sampling will correspondingly increase in size.
source: Because a proportional betting trajectory samples proportionate to the expected information, as the expected information diffuses, the excursions needed for its sampling will correspondingly increase in size.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation.

claim: In EIH, the spectral power profile of excursions is related to the length of time interval for which a trajectory is generated.
source: Second, in EIH, the spectral power profile of these excursions is related to the length of time interval for which a trajectory is generated (variable T in Figure 2, see Algorithm 1).
evidence: This is stated as a property of EIH with reference to a figure.

claim: In the strikes of the mottled sculpin, the entire strike is ballistic rather than a piece-wise open-loop ballistic strike.
source: In the strikes of the mottled sculpin, rather than a piece-wise open-loop ballistic strike, the entire strike is ballistic (Coombs and Conley, 1997).
evidence: This is stated as an example with citation.

claim: In electric fish, prey strikes are ballistic on time scales smaller than 115 ms but adaptive over longer time scales.
source: In contrast, prey strikes in electric fish are ballistic on time scales smaller than 115 ms but adaptive over longer time scales (MacIver et al., 2001; Snyder et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as an example with citations.

claim: In EIH, over the course of an enacted trajectory segment, changes in the expected information density due to new sensory observations have no effect; these will only be incorporated in the generation of the next trajectory segment.
source: In EIH, over the course of an enacted trajectory segment, changes in the expected information density due to new sensory observations similarly have no effect; these will only be incorporated in the generation of the next trajectory segment.
evidence: This is stated as a property of EIH.

claim: In EIH, perfect ergodicity is approached through the trade-off between the ergodic metric and the energy of movement within the prescribed trajectory time horizon T.
source: In EIH, perfect ergodicity is approached through the trade-off between the ergodic metric and the energy of movement within the prescribed trajectory time horizon T.
evidence: This is stated as a property of EIH.

claim: As T asymptotically approaches infinite duration, the system will approach perfect ergodicity as the ergodic measure approaches zero.
source: As T asymptotically approaches infinite duration, the system will approach perfect ergodicity as the ergodic measure approaches zero.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical property.

claim: As T asymptotically approaches zero duration, EIH will select a single direction to move to improve information.
source: Conversely, as T asymptotically approaches zero duration, EIH will select a single direction to move to improve information.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical property.

claim: Changing T between the bounds of zero and infinite duration will affect the frequency components of the sensing-related excursions in the context of exploring a bounded domain while searching for or tracking an object.
source: Changing T between these bounds will affect the frequency components of the sensing-related excursions in the context of exploring a bounded domain while searching for or tracking an object.
evidence: This is stated as a property of EIH.

claim: A shorter T causes the sensor to react more quickly in response to changes in the EID and hence leads to higher frequency components within sensing-related movements.
source: Because of these dynamics, a shorter T causes the sensor to react more quickly in response to changes in the EID and hence leads to higher frequency components within sensing-related movements.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation.

claim: The initial T used for the behavior simulations was chosen to fit the frequency of sensing-related oscillations observed in the weakly electric fish refuge tracking data.
source: The initial T (see Table 1) used for the behavior simulations was chosen to fit the frequency of sensing-related oscillations observed in the weakly electric fish refuge tracking data.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological choice.

claim: The same value of T was applied to mole and cockroach trials.
source: The same value was applied to mole and cockroach trials and reduced by a factor of five for the moth data due to the higher frequency content of the prescribed robotic flower movement.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological choice.

claim: T was reduced by a factor of five for the moth data due to the higher frequency content of the prescribed robotic flower movement.
source: The same value was applied to mole and cockroach trials and reduced by a factor of five for the moth data due to the higher frequency content of the prescribed robotic flower movement.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological choice.

claim: Information maximization and EIH emphasize different factors in target tracking.
source: Information maximization and EIH emphasize different factors in target tracking.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison in the discussion.

claim: If the initial location at which information maximization begins is near the wrong peak, information maximization will result in going to that peak and staying at that location.
source: First, if a scene is so noisy as to have fictive or real distractors, this will generate more than one peak in the probability distribution representing the estimated target location. If the initial location at which information maximization begins is near the wrong peak, information maximization will result in going to that peak (such as to the distractor in Figure 1B) and staying at that location.
evidence: This is stated as a problem with information maximization with reference to a figure.

claim: With ergodic harvesting, information across a specified region of interest will be sampled in proportion to its expected magnitude constrained by the energy expenditure needed to do so.
source: With ergodic harvesting, information across a specified region of interest will be sampled in proportion to its expected magnitude (Figure 1C) constrained by the energy expenditure needed to do so.
evidence: This is stated as a property of ergodic harvesting with reference to a figure.

claim: The poor agreement between infotactic trajectories and measured behavior indicates that the conjunction of three conditions (only one target of interest, the EID is normally distributed, and the signal is strong enough that false positives or other unmodeled uncertainties will not arise) rarely occurs in the behaviors examined.
source: For information maximization, if 1) there is only one target of interest; 2) the EID is normally distributed; and 3) the signal is strong enough that false positives or other unmodeled uncertainties will not arise, then information maximization will reduce the variance of the estimated location of the single target being sought and direct movement toward the true target location. We interpret the poor agreement between infotactic trajectories and measured behavior as indicating that the conjunction of these three conditions rarely occurs in the behaviors we examined.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Given that the behaviors examined were all highly constrained for experimental tractability, it seems likely that the conjunction of three conditions for information maximization to work well is even rarer in unconstrained three-dimensional animal behavior in nature.
source: Given that these behaviors were all highly constrained for experimental tractability, it seems likely to be even rarer in unconstrained three-dimensional animal behavior in nature.
evidence: This is stated as an inference.

claim: Information maximization leads to a cessation of movement when noise is dominating sensory input in high uncertainty scenarios since no additional information is expected to be gained in moving from the current location.
source: The second area where these two approaches have different emphases is highlighted in cases where noise is dominating sensory input in high uncertainty scenarios, as is common in naturalistic cases. Information maximization leads to a cessation of movement since no additional information is expected to be gained in moving from the current location (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated as a property of information maximization with reference to a figure.

claim: Energy-constrained proportional betting will result in a trajectory which covers the space when noise is dominating sensory input in high uncertainty scenarios.
source: Energy-constrained proportional betting will result in a trajectory which covers the space (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A): the expected information is flat, and a trajectory matching those statistics is one sweeping over the majority of the workspace at a density constrained by EIH's balancing of ergodicity with energy expenditure.
evidence: This is stated as a property of energy-constrained proportional betting with reference to a figure.

claim: For information maximization, coverage can only be an accidental byproduct of motions driven by information maximization.
source: For information maximization, coverage can only be an accidental byproduct of motions driven by information maximization.
evidence: This is stated as a property of information maximization.

claim: Appropriate exploration-exploitation trade-offs emerge organically within EIH.
source: Appropriate exploration-exploitation trade-offs emerge organically within EIH.
evidence: This is stated as a property of EIH.

claim: Fruit bats have been shown to oscillate their clicks from one side to the other of a target, rather than aiming their emissions directly at the target.
source: Fruit bats have been shown to oscillate their clicks from one side to the other of a target, rather than aiming their emissions directly at the target (Yovel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: Yovel et al., 2010 suggested that off-axis sensing behavior in bats arises from the bat aiming a peak in the maximum slope of the signal profile.
source: Yovel et al., 2010 suggested that this off-axis sensing behavior arises from the bat aiming a peak in the maximum slope of the signal profile (similar to the behavior of infotaxis, Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated with citation and reference to a figure.

claim: The maximum slope of the sonar beam intensity distribution does not necessarily, or even typically, correspond to a peak in the EID.
source: However, this analysis only provides a partial connection to information maximization, because the maximum slope of the sonar beam intensity distribution does not necessarily, or even typically, correspond to a peak in the EID.
evidence: This is stated as a critique.

claim: The main difference between the maximum slope of the sonar beam intensity distribution and the EID is that the EID accounts for the belief distribution that describes where the target might be and the uncertainty associated with that estimate.
source: The main difference between the two is that the EID accounts for the belief distribution—that describes where the target might be and the uncertainty associated with that estimate—whereas the sonar beam distribution only coincides with the EID if one assumes that the ground truth target is located at the peak of the sonar intensity.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation.

claim: The analyzed behavior in Yovel et al., 2010 is in a late phase of the sonar emission behavior, where the goal is mainly about maintaining an already good estimate of target location.
source: This means that the bats 'know' where the target is and are using sonar to maintain an estimate rather than globally searching for the target. This interpretation would indicate that the analyzed behavior in Yovel et al., 2010 is in a late phase of the sonar emission behavior, where the goal is mainly about maintaining an already good estimate of target location.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation.

claim: EIH performs well in the early stages of search behavior, when the target location is very uncertain and the EID plays a dominant role in behavior.
source: In contrast, EIH performs well in the early stages of search behavior, when the target location is very uncertain and the EID plays a dominant role in behavior.
evidence: This is stated as a property of EIH.

claim: In all the EIH simulations presented, the simulation began with a uniform prior for the belief, the highest level of uncertainty about target location possible.
source: In all the EIH simulations presented here, for example, the simulation began with a uniform prior for the belief, the highest level of uncertainty about target location possible.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological choice.

claim: Another hypothesis is that active sensing movements arise from the animal adapting its closed-loop tracking gain response to a reduction in signal contrast.
source: Another hypothesis is that active sensing movements arise from the animal adapting its closed-loop tracking gain response to a reduction in signal contrast (Borst et al., 2005; Ghose and Moss, 2006; Maimon et al., 2010; Biswas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: The gain adaptation hypothesis is underspecified, in the sense that critical components are missing to formulate an algorithm that generates predictive trajectories.
source: However, this gain adaptation hypothesis is underspecified, in the sense that critical components are missing to formulate an algorithm that generates predictive trajectories.
evidence: This is stated as a critique.

claim: If gain adaptation is implemented with a Bayesian filter and a process is specified to generate oscillatory motion around targets according to the variance of the belief as a measure of uncertainty, then in the narrow context of a single target with no distractors, such an algorithm can be tuned to behave similarly to EIH.
source: If gain adaptation is implemented with a Bayesian filter and a process is specified to generate oscillatory motion around targets according to the variance of the belief as a measure of uncertainty, then in the narrow context of a single target with no distractors (neither real nor fictive due to high uncertainty), such an algorithm can be tuned to behave similarly to EIH.
evidence: This is stated as a conditional statement.

claim: In more realistic scenarios, there is no apparent mechanism in gain adaptation to address real or fictive distractors, a capability of EIH.
source: However, in more realistic scenarios, there is no apparent mechanism to address real or fictive distractors, a capability of EIH we elaborate on further below.
evidence: This is stated as a critique.

claim: Khan et al., 2012 show that in rat odor tracking behavior only about 12% of the trajectory qualifies as edge-tracking.
source: Khan et al., 2012 show that in rat odor tracking behavior only about 12% of the trajectory qualifies as edge-tracking, suggesting that the rat's zig-zagging trajectory is not centered on the edge of the trail—as predicted by the information maximization hypothesis—but rather on the middle of the odor trail, consistent with ergodic harvesting.
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: The rat's zig-zagging trajectory is not centered on the edge of the trail but rather on the middle of the odor trail, consistent with ergodic harvesting.
source: Khan et al., 2012 show that in rat odor tracking behavior only about 12% of the trajectory qualifies as edge-tracking, suggesting that the rat's zig-zagging trajectory is not centered on the edge of the trail—as predicted by the information maximization hypothesis—but rather on the middle of the odor trail, consistent with ergodic harvesting.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation with citation.

claim: Khan et al. introduced a model for odor tracking that instructs the sensor to move forward and laterally at a fixed velocity and make decisions to switch the direction of lateral movements based on specific events of sensor measurement and position.
source: They also introduced a model for odor tracking that instructs the sensor to move forward and laterally at a fixed velocity and make decisions to switch the direction of lateral movements based on specific events of sensor measurement and position.
evidence: This is stated as a description of a model.

claim: Although the Khan et al. model could in principle be adjusted to fit the trajectories of animal tracking under weak signal, their zig-zag sensing-related movements are explicitly programmed to appear based on ad-hoc strategies.
source: Although their model could in principle be adjusted to fit the trajectories of animal tracking under weak signal, their zig-zag sensing-related movements are explicitly programmed to appear based on ad-hoc strategies.
evidence: This is stated as a critique.

claim: The Khan et al. model makes the model less generalizable and yields little insight into the underlying mechanism.
source: This makes the model less generalizable and yields little insight into the underlying mechanism.
evidence: This is stated as a critique.

claim: The sensing-related movements that arise from EIH are not programmed as such but emerge due to the principle of energy-constrained proportional betting.
source: In contrast, the sensing-related movements that arise from EIH are not programmed as such but emerge due to the principle of energy-constrained proportional betting.
evidence: This is stated as a property of EIH.

claim: The Khan et al. model lacks the ability to address distractors since the movement strategy is not based on the belief or EID map, whereas EIH naturally provides coverage in these scenarios.
source: In addition, the Khan et al. model lacks the ability to address distractors, as shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, since the movement strategy is not based on the belief or EID map, whereas EIH naturally provides coverage in these scenarios.
evidence: This is stated as a critique with reference to figures.

claim: Rucci and Victor, 2015 and Stamper et al., 2012 propose that active sensing movements are the outcome of an animal actively matching the spatial-temporal dynamics of upstream neural processing.
source: Finally, Rucci and Victor, 2015 and Stamper et al., 2012 propose that active sensing movements are the outcome of an animal actively matching the spatial-temporal dynamics of upstream neural processing—a process by which the movement serves as a 'whitening filter' (Rucci and Victor, 2015) or 'high-pass filter' (Stamper et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: Sensing-related movements could be for preventing perceptual fading, which has similarities to the high pass filter hypothesis in that motion is to counter sensory adaptation.
source: Sensing-related movements could be for preventing perceptual fading (Kunapareddy and Cowan, 2018), which has similarities to the high pass filter hypothesis in that motion is to counter sensory adaptation, a high pass filter-like phenomena.
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: Evidence for the perceptual fading hypothesis during tracking behaviors is lacking.
source: Although evidence for the perceptual fading hypothesis during tracking behaviors is lacking, EIH shows good agreement with animal behavior without any mechanism for sensory adaptation.
evidence: This is stated as an observation.

claim: EIH shows good agreement with animal behavior without any mechanism for sensory adaptation.
source: Although evidence for the perceptual fading hypothesis during tracking behaviors is lacking, EIH shows good agreement with animal behavior without any mechanism for sensory adaptation.
evidence: This is stated as a finding.

claim: Similar to the gain adaptation hypothesis, the high-pass filter hypothesis is also missing key components for trajectory prediction.
source: Similar to the gain adaptation hypothesis, the high-pass filter hypothesis is also missing key components for trajectory prediction.
evidence: This is stated as a critique.

claim: When implemented with the missing components, including a Bayesian filter and a feedback process that generates trajectories that match the desired spatial-temporal dynamics, the high-pass and whitening-filter hypotheses do not conflict with EIH in single target cases with low uncertainty.
source: Nonetheless, when implemented with the missing components, including a Bayesian filter and a feedback process that generates trajectories that match the desired spatial-temporal dynamics (Biswas et al., 2018), the high-pass and whitening-filter hypotheses do not conflict with EIH in single target cases with low uncertainty.
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: EIH predicts a preferred frequency band for sensing-related movements that may match the preferred spectral power of upstream neural processing.
source: This is because EIH also predicts a preferred frequency band for sensing-related movements that may match the preferred spectral power of upstream neural processing.
evidence: This is stated as a property of EIH.

claim: A capability of EIH that differentiates it from prior theories and that naturally arises from its distributed sampling approach is its ability to reject distractors and sample multiple targets.
source: Given the above discussion, a capability of EIH that differentiates it from prior theories and that naturally arises from its distributed sampling approach is its ability to reject distractors and sample multiple targets.
evidence: This is stated as a property of EIH.

claim: The live animal experimental data analyzed did not feature either real distractors or multiple targets.
source: The live animal experimental data we analyzed did not feature either real distractors (here defined as objects having a distinguishably different observation model from that of the target) or multiple targets (multiple objects with identical observation models).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the data.

claim: The EIH simulations suggest that sensing-related motions sometimes occur for rejection of fictive distractors while animals track single objects.
source: Nonetheless, the EIH simulations suggest that sensing-related motions sometimes occur for rejection of fictive distractors while animals track single objects.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from simulations.

claim: A fictive distractor emerges when the current belief for the target's location becomes multi-peaked.
source: A fictive distractor emerges when the current belief for the target's location becomes multi-peaked; each peak away from the true target's location is then a fictive distractor (illustrated by arrow in Figure 2I).
evidence: This is stated as a definition with reference to a figure.

claim: Fictive distractors arise in both the strong and weak signal conditions, but result in small amplitude excursions in the strong signal conditions because of the higher confidence of observations.
source: Fictive distractors arise in both the strong and weak signal conditions, but result in small amplitude excursions in the strong signal conditions because of the higher confidence of observations.
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: In simulated tracking behavior, the other source of sensing-related movements beside fictive distractor inspection is the increased spread of the EID as signals weaken.
source: In simulated tracking behavior, the other source of sensing-related movements beside fictive distractor inspection is the increased spread of the EID as signals weaken, as earlier discussed.
evidence: This is stated as a finding.

claim: False positive rejection has the signature of a digression from the nominal tracking trajectory; this digression ends when one or more samples have been received indicating there is no object present at the spurious belief peak.
source: False positive rejection has the signature of a digression from the nominal tracking trajectory; this digression ends when one or more samples have been received indicating there is no object present at the spurious belief peak, which then brings the believed target location back to somewhere closer to the true target position (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated as a description with reference to a figure.

claim: With a physical distractor, a digression should occur, but the incoming sensory signals support the hypothesis that the object being detected has a different observation model from that of the target, rather than the absence of an object.
source: In contrast, with a physical distractor, a digression should occur, but the incoming sensory signals support the hypothesis that the object being detected has a different observation model from that of the target, rather than the absence of an object.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction.

claim: EIH is able to locate the desired target while rejecting a simulated stationary physical distractor.
source: Figure 2—figure supplement 1 shows a simulated stationary physical distractor in addition to a stationary target. EIH is able to locate the desired target while rejecting the distractor.
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to a figure.

claim: Infotaxis stalls as it gets trapped at one of the information maximizing peaks and fails to reject the distractor.
source: In comparison, Figure 2—figure supplement 1 shows that infotaxis stalls as it gets trapped at one of the information maximizing peaks and fails to reject the distractor.
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to a figure.

claim: A prior robotics study experimentally tested how EIH responded to the presence of a physical distractor and showed that an electrolocation robot initially sampled the distractor but eventually rejected it.
source: This result buttresses a finding in a prior robotics study, where we experimentally tested how EIH responded to the presence of a physical distractor and showed that an electrolocation robot initially sampled the distractor but eventually rejected it (Figure 8 of Miller et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: If EIH has two targets, it maintains good tracking with an oscillatory motion providing coverage for both of the targets.
source: If, instead of a distractor and a target, EIH has two targets, the advantage of EIH's sampling the workspace proportional to the information density is particularly well highlighted. A simulation of this condition is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2. EIH maintains good tracking with an oscillatory motion providing coverage for both of the targets.
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to a figure.

claim: Infotaxis gets stuck at the location of the first target and fails to detect the presence of the other target when there are two targets.
source: As seen in Figure 2—figure supplement 2, such coverage is not a feature of infotaxis, which gets stuck at the location of the first target and fails to detect the presence of the other target.
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to a figure.

claim: Tracking multiple targets with different observation models requires a simple adjustment to the calculation of the EID that has been explored elsewhere.
source: A final case to consider is multiple targets with different (rather than identical) observation models. Tracking in such cases requires a simple adjustment to the calculation of the EID that we have explored elsewhere (Equation 13 of Miller et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: There is a clear need for animal tracking data in the presence of physical distractors or multiple targets in order to better understand whether EIH predicts sensory organ motion better than the gain adaptation or high-pass filtering theories in these cases.
source: While these preliminary simulations exploring how EIH performs with multiple targets and distractors are promising, it points to a clear need for animal tracking data in the presence of physical distractors or multiple targets (and in 2-D or 3-D behaviors: Appendix 6) in order to better understand whether EIH predicts sensory organ motion better than the gain adaptation or high-pass filtering theories in these cases.
evidence: This is stated as a need for future work.

claim: The sensor or whole-body sensing-related movements observed in the results is for proportional betting with regard to sensory system-specific EIDs—for electrosense, olfaction, and vision.
source: The sensor or whole-body sensing-related movements we observe in our results is for proportional betting with regard to sensory system-specific EIDs—for electrosense, olfaction, and vision.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the findings.

claim: To implement EIH, one needs to store at least a belief encoding knowledge about the target.
source: To implement EIH, one needs to store at least a belief encoding knowledge about the target.
evidence: This is stated as a requirement for implementation.

claim: The Bayesian filter update in EIH has the Markovian property, meaning that only the most recent belief is required to be stored.
source: The Bayesian filter update in EIH has the Markovian property, meaning that only the most recent belief is required to be stored.
evidence: This is stated as a property of EIH.

claim: The EID is derived from the belief and only used for every generated trajectory segment update, hence does not need to be stored.
source: The EID, moreover, is derived from the belief and only used for every generated trajectory segment update, hence does not need to be stored.
evidence: This is stated as a property of EIH.

claim: While the memory needs of EIH are low, trajectory synthesis requires computing the distance from ergodicity between candidate trajectories and the EID, a potentially complex calculation.
source: While the memory needs of EIH are low, trajectory synthesis requires computing the distance from ergodicity between candidate trajectories and the EID, a potentially complex calculation (Materials and methods, Appendix 3).
evidence: This is stated as a property of EIH.

claim: The complexity of the calculation in EIH may not be indicative of the complexity of implementation in biology.
source: However, the complexity of our calculation may not be indicative of the complexity of implementation in biology.
evidence: This is stated as a caveat.

claim: A recent study suggests that a predictive map of future state is encoded in grid cells of the entorhinal cortex through spatial decomposition on a low-dimensionality basis set—a process similar to the calculation of the ergodic metric.
source: For instance, a recent study (Stachenfeld et al., 2017) suggests that a predictive map of future state is encoded in grid cells of the entorhinal cortex through spatial decomposition on a low-dimensionality basis set—a process similar to the calculation of the ergodic metric (Appendix 3).
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: In weakly electric fish, electroreceptor afferents have power law adaptation in their firing rate in response to sensory input.
source: In weakly electric fish, electroreceptor afferents have power law adaptation in their firing rate in response to sensory input (Drew and Abbott, 2006; Clarke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: Power law adaptation makes the response of electroreceptor afferents invariant to the speed of the target.
source: This makes their response invariant to the speed of the target (Clarke et al., 2013) and hence similar to the simulated sensory input used to drive EIH.
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: The power law adaptation results in a very strong response at the reversal point during whole-body oscillations.
source: The power law adaptation also results in a very strong response at the reversal point during whole-body oscillations (Figure 5 of Clarke et al., 2014), a response generated by hindbrain-midbrain feedback loops (Clarke and Maler, 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: Given the importance of an increased rate of reversals as signals become weaker in the fish tracking data and EIH simulations, and EIH's invariance to speed, the hindbrain area along with feedback loops to the midbrain are a worthwhile target for future work on the biological basis of EIH.
source: Given the importance of an increased rate of reversals as signals become weaker in the fish tracking data and EIH simulations, and EIH's invariance to speed, the hindbrain area along with feedback loops to the midbrain are a worthwhile target for future work on the biological basis of EIH.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion for future work.

claim: Energy-constrained proportional betting trajectories show good agreement with the trajectories of animals whose targets are within sensing range.
source: Energy-constrained proportional betting trajectories show good agreement with the trajectories of animals whose targets are within sensing range.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the findings.

claim: Foraging theory, such as Charnov's marginal value theorem, has modeled animals with random displacements—a situation in which the statistics of resources in the habitat dominates, while whether the resource is within sensing range is not considered to play a role.
source: Foraging theory, such as Charnov's marginal value theorem (Charnov, 1976), has modeled animals with random displacements—a situation in which the statistics of resources in the habitat dominates, while whether the resource is within sensing range (or engages learning or memory systems) is not considered to play a role.
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: Lévy walk foraging is only predictive in information-scarce and low resource density contexts.
source: Lévy walk foraging is only predictive in information-scarce and low resource density contexts (Wosniack et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: The turbulent structure of wind-borne odors give rise to Lévy-flight like displacements in seabird navigation.
source: Newer work bridges the gap (Namboodiri et al., 2016; Kolling et al., 2012), such as showing that the turbulent structure of wind-borne odors give rise to Lévy-flight like displacements in seabird navigation (Reynolds et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: Nematode turning movements while looking for food is not stochastic, as previously believed, but rather predictable from recent sensory experience.
source: that nematode turning movements while looking for food is not stochastic, as previously believed, but rather predictable from recent sensory experience (Calhoun et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: Planning in volatile environments leverages patchy habitat statistics with processing over the cognitive map and visual sensorium.
source: and that planning in volatile environments leverages patchy habitat statistics with processing over the cognitive map and visual sensorium (Mugan and MacIver, 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: A common interpretation of body or sensor organ movements away from the assumed singular goal trajectory is that this reflects noise in perceptual or motor processes.
source: As in the case of fixational eye movements (Rucci and Victor, 2015), a common interpretation of body or sensor organ movements away from the assumed singular goal trajectory is that this reflects noise in perceptual or motor processes.
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: Ergodic harvesting presents a competing hypothesis: gathering information in uncertain complex environments means the system should be observed to move away from the singular goal trajectory.
source: Ergodic harvesting presents a competing hypothesis: gathering information in uncertain complex environments means the system should be observed to move away from the singular goal trajectory.
evidence: This is stated as a competing hypothesis.

claim: These excursions occur as predicted by EIH, including the possibility of multiple targets, and thus increase in size when uncertainty increases.
source: These excursions occur as predicted by EIH, including the possibility of multiple targets, and thus increase in size when uncertainty increases.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction of EIH.

claim: An occlusion may corrupt signal quality at a location otherwise predicted to have high target information.
source: An occlusion may corrupt signal quality at a location otherwise predicted to have high target information.
evidence: This is stated as a source of uncertainty.

claim: Other signal generators in the environment may emit confusing signals, or the location may be contaminated by a fictive distractor arising from unmodeled uncertainty.
source: Other signal generators in the environment may emit confusing signals, or the location may be contaminated by a fictive distractor arising from unmodeled uncertainty.
evidence: This is stated as a source of uncertainty.

claim: The opportunity to visit another location in space that is statistically independent—yet contains a similar amount of predicted information—gives an animal an opportunity to mitigate unmodeled uncertainties through the expenditure of energy for movement.
source: Hence, the opportunity to visit another location in space that is statistically independent—yet contains a similar amount of predicted information—gives an animal an opportunity to mitigate unmodeled uncertainties through the expenditure of energy for movement.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation.

claim: Experiments in human visual search suggest that saccades are planned in a multi-stage manner for coverage of information towards the task-relevant goal rather than aiming for information maximization.
source: This is supported by experiments in human visual search suggesting that saccades are planned in a multi-stage manner for coverage of information towards the task-relevant goal rather than aiming for information maximization (Yang et al., 2016; Hoppe and Rothkopf, 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: A model to predict human visual scan paths found 70% of the measured fixation locations were efficient from an information maximization perspective, but there were many fixations (≈30%) that were not purely for maximizing information and attributed in part to perceptual or motor noise.
source: For example, a model to predict human visual scan paths found 70% of the measured fixation locations were efficient from an information maximization perspective, but there were many fixations (≈30%) that were not purely for maximizing information and attributed in part to perceptual or motor noise (Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: The apparently less efficient fixation locations are in fact the result of gambling on information through motion.
source: We hypothesize that these apparently less efficient fixation locations are in fact the result of gambling on information through motion.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis.

claim: It is possible that motor noise may aid coverage in a computationally inexpensive manner.
source: It is also possible that motor noise may aid coverage in a computationally inexpensive manner.
evidence: This is stated as a possibility.

claim: The role of motion in sensing is to mitigate the adverse impact of sensor properties.
source: The role of motion in this sensing setting is to mitigate the adverse impact of sensor properties.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation.

claim: If one is in an uncertain world full of surprises that cannot be anticipated, using energy to more fully measure the world's properties makes sense.
source: If, however, one is in an uncertain world full of surprises that cannot be anticipated, using energy to more fully measure the world's properties makes sense.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle.

claim: Energy-constrained proportional betting predicts amplified energy expenditure in response to large structural uncertainties.
